title: The 45-minute interview
intro: A system design interview is a structured conversation that you are expected to drive. The interviewer is not grading the diagram; they are grading how you think, what you prioritize, and whether they would trust you to lead this design with a real team. This playbook is the structure. Practice it until the structure is invisible and only the thinking shows.

timeline.goal: Turn a two-sentence prompt into a bounded problem with agreed functional and non-functional requirements.
do: Restate the problem in one sentence and confirm it.
Ask who the users are and what the three most important actions are.
Propose what is in scope and explicitly what is out, and get a nod.
Ask the questions whose answers change the design: scale, read/write, latency, consistency, geography.
Write the requirements where both of you can see them.
avoid: Asking twenty questions without proposing answers; staff candidates propose and confirm.
Accepting 'as scalable as possible' as a requirement.
timeline.say: 'Let me make sure I am solving the right problem. I am going to assume X, Y, and Z are in scope and leave W out; does that match what you had in mind?'

timeline.goal: Produce the four or five numbers that shape the architecture and interpret them out loud.
do: Derive RPS from users and actions; state average and peak.
Derive storage from write rate and record size; state one year and five years.
State the read/write ratio and the hottest access pattern.
Translate each number into a consequence: 'that fits one primary', 'that needs a cache', 'that forces sharding'.
avoid: Precision. Round to one significant figure and move on.
Estimating things that do not change the design.
timeline.say: 'Roughly 5K writes a second at peak, which a single Postgres handles, but at this growth rate we cross the line in about two years, so I will design the data layer so that transition is possible.'

timeline.goal: Draw the simplest system that satisfies the requirements end to end, with the data flow for the top two or three operations.
do: Start with clients, an API layer, the services that matter, the primary store, and the async path.
Walk one read and one write through the diagram, naming every hop.
Define the core API and the core data model briefly.
Call out the one or two components you expect to be the hard part and say you will return to them.
avoid: Drawing every box you know. Each box must earn its place with a requirement.
Going deep before the whole picture exists.
timeline.say: 'This is deliberately simple. The interesting problems are the fan-out on write and the consistency of the counter; I want to spend most of our time there.'

timeline.goal: Demonstrate depth on the two or three components that carry the most risk, with explicit tradeoffs and numbers.
do: Pick the deep dive that matters most, or let the interviewer steer, and go one level down: data model, algorithm, failure handling.
For every choice, name the alternative and the condition under which you would switch.
Address scale explicitly: what breaks at 10x, and what you would change.
Address failure explicitly: what happens when this component is slow, down, or partitioned.
avoid: Listing technologies without the reasoning that picks one.
Hand-waving consistency. Say exactly what a reader can see after a write.
timeline.say: 'There are two ways to do this. Option A is simpler and fine until about 50K subscribers per topic. Past that, B. Given our numbers, I would ship A with the interface shaped so B is a swap, not a rewrite.'

timeline.goal: Show you have run systems: observability, deploys, security, cost, and the migration path when requirements change.
do: Name the three alerts that would page a human and the SLO behind each.
Say how a change ships safely: flags, canary, rollback.
Name the dominant cost line and one lever to cut it.
Describe the next architectural transition and what triggers it.
avoid: Treating this as optional. It is where staff candidates separate from senior ones.
timeline.say: 'In production, the first thing I expect to bite us is replication lag making the user's own write disappear, so I would ship read-your-writes pinning on day one and alert on lag over two seconds.'

timeline.goal: Leave the interviewer with a crisp picture and the sense that you know what you do not know.
do: Summarize the design in three sentences: the shape, the hard part, the key tradeoff.
Name one thing you would want to validate with real data before committing.
Ask the interviewer what they would push on, if time remains.
avoid: Introducing a new component in the last two minutes.
timeline.say: 'To summarize: write-time fan-out with a read-time merge for high-follower accounts, Postgres sharded by user with Redis timelines, Kafka for the async path. The riskiest assumption is the 100:1 read ratio; I would instrument that in week one.'

senior: Produces a working design that meets the stated requirements.
Knows the standard components and uses them correctly.
Handles the deep dive the interviewer picks.
staff: Drives the conversation: proposes scope, quantifies unprompted, chooses the deep dives.
Reasons from numbers and constraints to decisions, and names the number that would flip each decision.
Keeps the design as simple as the requirements allow and resists adding components without a reason.
Designs the evolution: what breaks at 10x, which transition comes first, how it is migrated without downtime.
Treats failure, operations, security, and cost as part of the design, not an appendix.
Considers the organization: team boundaries, ownership, on-call load, what a platform must provide.
Says 'I would not build that' when it is true, and explains what to do instead.
Is honest about uncertainty and says what they would measure to resolve it.

phrases: 'The number that decides this is X. Let me estimate it.'
'I am going to keep this simple on purpose and spend our time where the risk is.'
'This works until roughly N. Past that, we would change Y, and here is how the migration goes.'
'If this component is slow rather than down, here is what the caller does.'
'That is a product decision with a cost; here are the two options and what each buys.'
'I have seen this fail in production because of Z, so I would add W from day one.'
'The alternative is A. I would switch to it if B became true.'
'What I would want to validate first is...'
redFlags: Starting to draw before any requirement is agreed.
Microservices, Kafka, or Cassandra proposed without a number that requires them.
A single global latency or availability target for all operations.
No answer for 'what if this box fails' on any box.
A cache with no invalidation story, or a queue with no idempotency story.
Sharding without naming the key and the query it makes expensive.
Never mentioning how a change gets deployed or how you would know it broke.
Running out of time with no deep dive done.

items: Who are the users and what are the top three things they do?
How many daily active users, and what is the growth trajectory?
What is the read-to-write ratio for the main operations?
What latency does the main interactive operation need, at p99?
Which operations need strong consistency, and which can be stale for a few seconds?
Where are the users, and are there data residency constraints?
What is the budget or cost sensitivity, and what is the team size?
Is this greenfield, or are we evolving an existing system?
What happens when this component is slow, not down?
What is the blast radius of a bad deploy here?
How does a user see their own write immediately?
What is the hottest key, and what happens to it?
How would you migrate off this choice if it turns out wrong?
What would you cut if the budget halved?
Which three alerts page a human?
What did you leave out, and why?
Our monolith hurts and we have 80 engineers. What do we do this year?
One tenant is 30 percent of our load. Fix it without losing them.
Add an LLM feature to this product; cost and safety matter.
We need to be in the EU by Q3 with residency guarantees.
Move the orders table to a new store with zero downtime.
Our p99 doubled after the last three releases. Where do you start?
Design the on-call and reliability program for this system.
